Batch processing.
By the end of this part, you'll know the two tests a job must pass before it goes to batch, and how to collect the results without losing any.
Let's start with a picture.
Posting letters in the evening is cheaper than sending each one by courier.
But you don't post the key your colleague is standing at the door waiting for.
You courier the key.
And you post the monthly newsletter.
That's the whole decision in this part.
Anthropic offers a cheaper, overnight-style service for work nobody is waiting on.
So the question is always the same.
Is anyone standing there waiting for this result?
The technical name is the Message Batches API.
That's the application programming interface for batch processing.
You submit many requests at once, and collect the results later.
Here are the facts the exam uses.
One at a time.
One.
It costs fifty percent of standard rates.
Two.
It uses the same model and parameters.
So output quality is the same.
Three.
A batch holds up to one hundred thousand requests, or two hundred and fifty-six megabytes, whichever comes first.
Four.
Most batches finish within an hour.
But the hard ceiling is twenty-four hours.
And there's no guaranteed delivery time inside that window.
Five.
Requests still unprocessed at twenty-four hours end as expired.
A few more facts.
Six.
Results come back as a stream of newline-separated JSON.
And they stay available for twenty-nine days.
Seven.
Streaming output is not available inside batch requests.
And eight.
Batch requests do support tool definitions, system prompts, images, extended thinking, and prompt caching.
So the batch discount stacks with the caching savings we'll cover in the chapter on context management.
There are two tests for whether batch fits.
And you need both.
The first test is latency tolerance.
That's the deciding axis.
Is a user, or a pipeline, blocked waiting on this result?
If yes, use the standard synchronous service.
A pre-merge check.
Live chat.
A two-minute routing target.
A four-hour compliance window.
All synchronous.
And design to the worst case, not the typical case.
"Most finish within an hour" doesn't satisfy a four-hour deadline.
Why?
Because the documented ceiling is twenty-four hours.
The second test is whether the task is a single turn.
Here's the plain version.
Dropping off a list of questions at a catering company works when each question can be answered on its own.
It doesn't work for a conversation where each answer decides the next question.
Because nobody is there to reply.
In exam terms, a batch request is one request and one response.
If the model asks to call a tool, nobody is listening to run it and send the result back.
So an agent loop can't run inside a batch.
That's a loop where the model reads a file, decides what to open next, and reads again.
Now a subtle point.
Two sources can seem to clash here.
The notes say batch requests support tool use.
That's true.
You can define tools, force a single extraction call, and read the answer from that one response.
What batch can't do is host a multi-turn loop that needs your code to execute tools and reply.
So, hold on to this line.
If the answer needs one forced tool call, batch is fine.
If it needs back-and-forth, it isn't.
Two more properties dominate correct design.
First.
Results are not ordered.
You attach a custom_id to every request.
It's between one and sixty-four characters, of letters, numbers, hyphens and underscores.
And you join results back on it.
Never on position.
Code that pairs result number N with input number N is wrong, even when it passes tests.
And it produces the worst class of bug.
Correct data, attached to the wrong record.
Second.
Failure is per request, not per batch.
The batch's processing_status moves through in_progress, possibly canceling, and then ended.
And here's the catch.
Ended means every request reached a final state.
It doesn't mean every request succeeded.
Each result carries one of four types.
Succeeded.
Errored.
Canceled.
Or expired.
And only succeeded results are billed.
So the right handler switches on all four.
It loads the successes.
It re-queues the recoverable failures.
And it alarms on the rates.
The notes offer a pattern worth remembering.
Hold on to this line.
Treat the batch boundary as a checkpoint, not a transaction.
Here's the sequence.
Submit.
Poll until ended.
Stream the results.
Join on custom_id.
Run your tier two and tier three checks from part four on each success.
And route validation failures, plus every errored and expired result, into the next batch or a human queue.
Quick recap before the questions.
Two tests, in order.
Is anyone waiting?
Is it a single turn?
Then join on custom_id, and treat ended as "finished," not "succeeded."
Right.
Four practice questions.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
Every pull request triggers an AI review that must pass before merge.
Reviews finish in a few minutes.
Finance proposes batch for the discount, noting most batches finish within an hour.
The team also runs a nightly full-repository security audit that nobody waits on.
What should the architect do?
Take a second.
The answer.
Keep the pre-merge reviews synchronous, because batch has no guaranteed delivery time.
And move the nightly audit to batch.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: move the reviews to batch, because typical turnaround fits the working day.
Why?
That designs to the average, and ignores the ceiling.
Wrong: poll every minute.
Why?
That tells you sooner that a batch finished.
Not that it finished sooner.
Wrong: keep both synchronous, because "batch produces lower-quality reviews."
Why?
That's factually wrong.
Same model, same quality.
The disqualifier is timing.
Question two.
This is the one that catches strong candidates.
Here's the scenario.
A nightly job has an agent explore each repository, through repeated file-read and search tool calls.
It decides what to open next from what it read.
Then it writes an architecture summary.
Nobody reads the summaries until morning.
Finance wants batch.
What's the right call?
Take a second.
The answer.
Keep it on the standard service.
Each run is a multi-turn tool loop that a batch request can't service.
Latency alone would favour batch.
And that's exactly what makes this tempting.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: move it as is, because nothing waits.
Why?
It passes the first test, and fails the second.
Wrong: batch with streaming enabled.
Why?
Streaming isn't available in batches.
And it wouldn't supply the missing tool turn anyway.
Wrong: split into many small batches.
Why?
That adds no conversation turn.
And it multiplies the tracking work.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A nightly job extracts fields from about twenty thousand invoices, by batch.
The loader waits for processing_status to reach ended.
Then it writes every result it receives.
Analysts find one to two percent of invoices missing after heavy nights.
With no errors logged.
What's the best fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Switch on each result type.
Load succeeded.
Re-queue errored or expired.
And alarm on the failure rates.
Here's the picture.
A delivery van returning to the depot means every parcel has been dealt with.
Not that every parcel was delivered.
If nobody checks the returns shelf, those customers never get their parcels.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: split into smaller batches.
Why?
Failure is already per request, so it buys nothing.
And re-running whole batches reprocesses successes.
Wrong: poll more often.
Why?
That changes when you learn the batch ended.
Not what succeeded.
Wrong: write placeholder rows full of nulls.
Why?
That hides the failure, as though the invoices were blank.
And they're never actually processed.
On splitting, the notes add a useful nuance.
Splitting one job into many small batches, "to get results sooner and limit blast radius," is mostly illusory.
Why?
It doesn't speed up the queue.
And a single poison input already fails only itself.
What splitting does buy is more polling, more batch identifiers, and more joins.
Each one a chance to lose a slice.
So what are the defensible reasons to split?
Operational ones.
Such as aligning batches to tenant boundaries, or to schema versions.
Question four.
This one is choose two.
Here's the scenario.
A support organisation wants to move suitable work to batch.
There are five options.
One.
Live chat drafting, while the customer waits.
Two.
Overnight re-tagging of last quarter's closed tickets.
Three.
Weekly quality scoring of chat transcripts, for a Monday report.
Four.
Routing each ticket, under a two-minute target.
Five.
A refund agent that calls order-lookup tools over several turns.
Which two are good fits?
Take a second.
The answers.
The overnight re-tagging, and the weekly scoring.
Both pass both tests.
Nobody waits on any single result.
And each request is one turn.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: live chat, and two-minute routing.
Why?
Someone is waiting.
Wrong: the refund agent.
Why?
It needs a tool loop.
Think of the office laundry.
You happily send it to a cheap overnight service.
But not the shirt you need in ten minutes.
And you can't send it anything that needs you to answer questions halfway through.
A contrast to lock this in.
Batch versus real-time.
Real-time buys responsiveness.
Batch buys a fifty percent discount.
So pay for responsiveness only when someone consumes it.
And the two tests run in order.
First, is anyone waiting?
Second, is it a single turn?
A job must pass both.
And the words in a question that should switch this part on.
"Must pass before merge," "customer waiting," "two-minute target," or "four-hour compliance window."
All of those mean synchronous.
"Overnight," "nobody reads it until morning," "backfill," "weekly report."
Those point to batch.
Unless the stem also says "repeated tool calls," or "decides what to open next."
"Most batches finish within an hour."
That's bait.
"Missing records, no errors logged."
That means ended was read as success.
"Attached to the wrong record."
That means positional joining, instead of custom_id.
That's part five.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Batch only when nobody is waiting and each request is a single turn.
Then join on custom_id, and handle all four result types.
